snapshots.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
snapshots.subtitle: Wollstonecraft's central opponent
snapshots.body: The philosopher whose Emile argued that women should be educated only to please and serve men, a view Wollstonecraft names and dismantles across the book. She credits him with real consistency — he at least admitted a proper education would unfit women for the subjection he wanted to keep them in — even as she rejects his conclusion entirely.

snapshots.name: Dr. John Gregory
snapshots.subtitle: Author of A Father's Legacy to His Daughters
snapshots.body: The author of a popular conduct book advising young women to affect ignorance and hide their accomplishments to please men, which Wollstonecraft says she approaches "with affectionate respect" for its evident paternal solicitude, even while dissecting its advice as harmful.

snapshots.name: Dr. James Fordyce
snapshots.subtitle: Author of Sermons to Young Women
snapshots.body: The clergyman whose widely read Sermons to Young Women Wollstonecraft singles out for particular scorn — declaring she would dismiss them from a pupil's library at once, on account of their sentimental, patronizing tone toward female readers.

snapshots.name: John Milton
snapshots.subtitle: Paradise Lost's Eve, examined
snapshots.body: Cited for his description of Eve as formed for softness and sweet attractive grace — a characterization Wollstonecraft says she cannot make sense of except as one more instance of a great writer accepting, without examination, the received idea of woman's subordinate nature.

snapshots.name: Catharine Macaulay
snapshots.subtitle: The historian Wollstonecraft admires
snapshots.body: The historian Wollstonecraft calls the woman of the greatest abilities her country has produced, held up repeatedly as living proof that a woman's mind, properly cultivated, can command a respect independent of beauty or the usual feminine graces.

snapshots.name: The "Sexual Character"
snapshots.subtitle: The notion the book is written against
snapshots.body: The prevailing idea — stated in the Introduction as the book's central target — that women possess a separate, softer nature suited only to pleasing and obeying men, which Wollstonecraft argues is subversive of morality itself once examined honestly.

snapshots.name: Artificial Weakness
snapshots.subtitle: Degradation disguised as virtue
snapshots.body: The condition Wollstonecraft diagnoses in Chapter II: women degraded by mistaken notions of female excellence until they mistake a manufactured helplessness for a natural grace, a weakness she argues in turn breeds petty tyranny rather than genuine virtue.

snapshots.name: Rational Creatures
snapshots.subtitle: What the book insists women are
snapshots.body: The book's founding claim, argued in Chapter I: that women, no less than men, are rational creatures meant to rise toward excellence through the exercise of their own reason and virtue — not decorative dependents whose only purpose is to please.

snapshots.name: Modesty
snapshots.subtitle: Redefined against sexual virtue
snapshots.body: The subject of Chapter VII, which Wollstonecraft calls the sacred offspring of sensibility and reason: a quality of mind she insists on separating from the narrow, sex-specific bashfulness conduct writers had turned it into, treating it instead as a virtue proper to any rational being.

snapshots.name: National Education
snapshots.subtitle: The book's practical proposal
snapshots.body: The subject of Chapter XII: Wollstonecraft's proposal for public, coeducational schooling as the practical remedy for the degradation she has diagnosed — offered, she says, as hints rather than a finished system, but pressed as essential to reforming both sexes together.

mentions.text: Dr. Gregory's Legacy to his daughters
Milton describes our first frail mother
this artificial weakness produces a propensity to tyrannize
rational creatures produced, allowed to rise in excellency
Modesty! Sacred offspring of sensibility and reason
